activities.title: Computers, ethics and society
activities.description: Ten questions on artificial intelligence and machine learning, algorithmic bias, the digital divide, automation and employment, e-waste, accessibility and intellectual property. Written for Leaving Certificate Computer Science.

config.title: Computers, ethics and society
config.instructions: Several of these have more than one defensible-sounding answer — choose the one that is most accurate. Each question is worth 1 mark.

questions.stem: How does a machine learning system differ from a traditional rule-based program?

options.text: It does not need a computer to run.
It is always more accurate than a rule-based program.
It writes its own hardware.
Its behaviour is derived from patterns in training data rather than from rules written out by a programmer.

questions.stem: A company's CV-screening model rejects far more women than men. The training data was ten years of the company's own past hiring decisions. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The model was given too much data.
A programmer must have written a rule to reject women.
The model learned the biases present in the historical decisions it was trained on.
Machine learning cannot process text CVs.

questions.stem: What is meant by the digital divide?

options.text: The split between hardware engineers and software engineers.
The gap between those with reliable access to technology and connectivity and those without, which widens other inequalities.
The difference between analogue and digital signals.
The boundary between a company's internal network and the internet.

questions.stem: Why is the explainability of an automated decision system a genuine ethical concern?

options.text: If nobody can say why a loan or a place was refused, the decision cannot be challenged, audited or corrected.
Explainable systems always run faster.
It is impossible to test a system you cannot explain.
Users prefer systems with more documentation.

questions.stem: Which statement about automation and employment is best supported by the history of computing?

options.text: Automation always reduces the total number of jobs in an economy.
Automation has no effect on employment.
Automation only affects manual work, never office work.
Automation removes some kinds of work and creates others, but the people displaced are rarely the ones who fill the new roles.

questions.stem: Why is e-waste a significant environmental problem?

options.text: Electronic devices are biodegradable and release methane.
The plastic in devices is the only part that cannot be recycled.
Discarded devices contain both toxic materials and valuable recoverable metals, and much of it is exported to be dismantled in unsafe conditions.
E-waste takes up more space in landfill than any other waste stream.

questions.stem: A student finds a photograph online with no licence stated and uses it on a public website. What is the position?

options.text: Anything on the internet is free to reuse.
The photograph is automatically protected by copyright; permission or a licence is needed, so an openly licensed or public domain image should be used instead.
It is fine as long as the site is not making money.
It is fine as long as the photographer is credited.

questions.stem: Under GDPR, what must an organisation do before processing someone's personal data on the basis of consent?

options.text: Obtain consent that is freely given, specific and informed, and make it as easy to withdraw as to give.
Publish the data on its website.
Add a line about it somewhere in a long terms-and-conditions document.
Nothing, provided the data is stored securely.

questions.stem: Which change most improves a website for a user with a severe visual impairment?

options.text: Brighter colours throughout.
More images instead of text.
A larger logo in the header.
Meaningful alt text, proper heading structure and full keyboard navigation, so a screen reader can convey the page.

questions.stem: Video and audio of a real person can now be convincingly fabricated. What is the most serious societal consequence?

options.text: Video files will become much larger.
Editing software will become harder to use.
People can be shown saying things they never said, and — just as damaging — genuine recordings can be dismissed as fakes.
Cameras will need to be replaced more often.

q1.explanation: In a rule-based program a human states the logic; in machine learning the system infers it from examples. That is powerful for problems nobody can write rules for — recognising a face — and it is also why the data used for training determines what the system does, and why it can be hard to say why it did it.

q2.explanation: A model trained on past decisions reproduces the pattern in those decisions, including the unfair parts, without anyone writing a discriminatory rule. Removing the gender field does not fix it either, since other fields act as proxies. Amazon abandoned a real recruiting tool for exactly this reason.

q3.explanation: The divide runs along income, geography, age and disability, and it compounds: when schooling, banking and public services move online, the people already worst served lose the most. Rural broadband and device access in schools are the local face of it.

q4.explanation: A decision that affects someone's rights has to be contestable, and you cannot appeal a reason nobody can state. It is why GDPR gives a right to meaningful information about automated decisions, and why an accurate model can still be unacceptable in a high-stakes setting.

q5.explanation: Mechanisation and computerisation have repeatedly destroyed occupations and created others — the honest difficulty is the transition, which falls on particular people in particular places. Note that this wave reaches clerical, legal and creative work, so 'd' has not held for a long time.

q6.explanation: Lead, mercury and cadmium leach from dumped devices, while the gold and rare earths inside are lost unless recovered. Much e-waste is shipped abroad and stripped by hand over open fires. Repairability and longer replacement cycles cut the problem at source.

q7.explanation: Copyright is automatic on creation — no notice is needed for it to apply, so silence is not permission. Credit is a courtesy, not a licence, and non-commercial use is not a general exemption. Creative Commons and public domain sources exist precisely to make lawful reuse easy.

q8.explanation: GDPR sets a high bar: consent must be a genuine choice, tied to a stated purpose, and withdrawable at any time. Pre-ticked boxes and consent buried in terms and conditions do not qualify, and consent is only one of six lawful bases for processing.

q9.explanation: A screen reader user navigates by headings and links and never sees the layout, so structure and alt text are what carry the page. Accessibility work also helps everyone else — keyboard navigation, captions and clear structure improve the site for all users, and in the EU it is a legal requirement for public bodies.

q10.explanation: The second half is the subtler harm: once fabrication is plausible, any inconvenient recording can be waved away as a fake. That erosion of shared evidence is harder to repair than any single forged clip, and it is why provenance and watermarking are being taken seriously.
